newsitem.title: JAPAN: MINOR METALS - Molybdenum prices to Japan rising.
newsitem.headline: MINOR METALS - Molybdenum prices to Japan rising.

text.p: The price of molybdenum for Japanese buyers has jumped over the past month and is likely to continue to rise, but local end-users currently hold ample stocks and are not keen to buy, traders said on Tuesday.
Offer prices for molybdenum from European traders are now being quoted at $5.75 a lb on a C&F Japan basis, up from $3.30 at the end of August, they said. Molybdenum is used for steel making.

The molybdenum market was recently bolstered by a shortage of concentrate, a lack of Chinese offers and news that lower metal grades at Codelco's Chuquicamata mine in Chile would cause metal output to drop to around 30 million pounds this year from 37 million in 1995.
Japanese end-users rushed to buy molybdenum in 1995 when the price of the metal surged, and held about 3,266 tonnes of stocks at the end of last year, traders said.
They gradually adjusted their stockpiles this year and held nearly 2,913 tonnes at the end of June, which is equal to almost two months of domestic consumption, they said.
"The stocks are enough for Japan's immediate requirements, and end-users have no reason to buy at higher prices now," a minor metals trader at a Tokyo-based major trade house said.
Japanese traders said molybdenum is expected to move between $3.00 and $7.50 a lb in the near term. "I think the $6 level will be an immediate target," another minor metals trader said.
Minor metals traders in Hong Kong were sidelined on Tuesday due to China's National Day public holiday.
European bids for antimony were $2,200, but Chinese sellers were offering the metal at $2,300 a tonne on C&F Hong Kong.
Bid and offer prices for manganese showed a $100 per tonne gap, traders said, European bids were below $1,300 a tonne, but the Chinese were offering that price FOB at southern ports.
One European trader said up to half of China's 140 manganese producers have gone out of business because prices have fallen below the break-even point of $1,400 per tonne.

"There is plenty of material in Rotterdam," he said, "so anyone from Europe who wants it can get it there," the trader said. Prices for Chinese manganese in Rotterdam warehouses begin at $1,200 a tonne and fall from there, he said.
China's manganese production capacity stands at 80,000 tonnes a year, but actual production is around 50,000 tonnes, almost all for export, the trader said.
With the closure of plants in places such as Hunan province, due to summer flooding, production in 1996 will be even less, he said.

Traders said the quality of the Chinese product remained a problem. One trader said he had to travel to far-off northern Liaoning province to oversee ship loadings to make sure he got the quality he paid for.
